title: Don't Go Monolithic; the Agent Stack Is Stratifying
story_key: story|title:don t go monolithic the agent stack is stratifying
content_excerpt: The defensible asset in enterprise AI is not the model. It’s the organizational world model. Every major compute era decomposes into specialized layers with different winners at each level. Cloud split into IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS. The modern data stack split into ingestion, warehousing, transformation, and BI. Each time, specialists beat the generalists because each layer has its own economics: its own rate of change, capital requirements, and sources of lock-in. The enterprise AI agent stack is doing the same thing right now. Arvind Jain, the CEO of Glean, recently published a structural analysis of the emerging enterprise agent architecture that crystallized something I’d been thinking about. He describes a stack splitting into six layers (security, context, models, orchestration, agents, and interfaces), and each layer is defensible to a different degree. Glean sits in the context layer so the usual positioning caveats apply, but the structural argument is sound regardless of who makes it. The three sections below cover models converging toward shared infrastructure, the two depths of the context layer, and the compounding flywheel that context and orchestration form. The model layer is converging fastest toward commodity economics. Training costs scale roughly 2.4x per year , with current frontier runs costing hundreds of millions and billion-dollar training runs already underway , according to Anthropic’s Dario Amodei. Only a handful of organizations on Earth can operate at this scale: OpenAI, Google DeepMind, Anthropic, Meta, and a few others including xAI and Mistral. This is capital-intensive infrastructure, with the same structure as semiconductor fabs or cloud hyperscalers. I expect foundation models to become shared utilities, so no enterprise will build a moat on one. Companies already act on this. 37% of enterprises now use five or more models in production , up from 29% the prior year. Different tasks demand different models: Claude for code and tool use, GPT for extended reasoning, Gemini Flash for low-latency routing, specialized models for image generation and embeddings. Betting your enterprise stack on a single model provider carries the same risk as betting it on a single cloud. Open standards like Anthropic’s Model Context Protocol , now hosted by the Linux Foundation with 97 million monthly SDK downloads, and Google’s Agent-to-Agent protocol are making this multi-model enterprise AI architecture practical. title: Loose Ends: A check for unused code AI wrote or forgot to remove
story_key: story|title:loose ends a check for unused code ai wrote or forgot to remove
content_excerpt: Graph-powered liveness checks for AI-written code. Fails a pull request that leaves orphaned, superseded, or unreachable code. TypeScript, JavaScript, Python, Java. Coding agents write code fast, and they leave things behind: a helper that is never called, a UserServiceV2 sitting next to the UserService it replaced, a route that was unregistered while its handler stayed. Loose Ends checks every change before merge and reports, with evidence, whether the code it added or touched is still reachable from a real entry point. That is the express-api example after an agent-style change: a v2 service was added and wired in, the original was left behind, and an unused pagination helper was added. Loose Ends builds a Liveness Graph of TypeScript, JavaScript, Python, and Java code: imports, exports, re-exports, references between top-level declarations, dynamic imports, and package dependencies. It finds roots in package manifests, scripts, framework conventions (Next.js routes, Vite entries, browser extension manifests, serverless functions, tool configs, Django apps, pyproject entry points, server commands in Dockerfiles and Procfiles, Spring and Jakarta annotations, Android manifests and layouts), config, and tests. It analyzes the base and head revisions and reports only what the change did. Existing dead code never blocks a pull request. It is not an LLM guessing whether code looks unused, a general code reviewer, a formatter, or a security scanner. It does not claim that unobserved code is safe to delete, and it never deletes anything without deterministic evidence and a passing verification run. bench/RESULTS.md has the results on public repositories, including about 700 Python and Java commits replayed through check and a sweep of 30 popular repositories. Python and Java projects need no package.json . With Node installed, run npx loose-ends check from the repository root. The npm packages are published from GitHub Actions with provenance , so each version links back to the commit it was built from. check exits with 0 on pass, 1 on blocking findings, and 2 when it could not run. scan reports existing code instead of a change, so it uses orphaned (nothing reaches it) and test-only (only tests reach it), plus unused-dependency and uncertain . title: Sandbox resourcing: burst, don't reserve
summary: Why you're paying for capacity you aren't using, and how to pay only for what you use.
story_key: story|title:sandbox resourcing burst don t reserve
content_excerpt: Across Modal, a typical Sandbox spends more than half its life using less than 6% of its peak CPU. Take a coding agent: the Sandbox sits nearly idle while the model reasons about what to do next, and spikes only when the agent installs dependencies, runs tests, or builds the project. The same pattern shows up in other common Sandbox workloads: RL rollouts, evals, and app builders. Today, most sandboxes are priced based on a fixed-resource reservation model. Reservations are a poor fit for spiky work, for two reasons: We believe your bill should align with your workload, rising when it’s busy and falling when it’s idle. That’s why our Sandboxes burst: a Sandbox gets the CPU and memory it needs when your work spikes and gives them back when it is done. You pay for what you actually use. Every Sandbox bursts by default. Start with the base 0.125 cores and 128 MiB request and let your Sandbox grow as it needs. With active-resource pricing, you pay each second for what you use, with the small request as a floor. You can request more to guarantee it, but you’ll pay for those resources even when your Sandbox is idle. You can also set a limit to cap how far your Sandbox can burst; think of it as setting the size of the computer the Sandbox lives on. Most workloads don’t need to set a request or limit: use the default and burst from there. Because you pay for what you use, estimate your costs from average usage rather than peak usage: CPU cost ≈ runtime × CPU rate × average cores used Memory cost ≈ runtime × memory rate × average GiB used This average works for bursting Sandboxes because each second, a Sandbox is billed for the higher of its request and what it actually uses. Since the average sits well below the peak, customers with bursty workloads can end up paying a fraction of their typical reservation bill. Your Sandbox is guaranteed its request, which is small by default. When it bursts beyond that, it draws from a shared pool of the machine’s idle capacity, which Modal’s scheduler keeps free on every machine. It works because of the law of averages. Sandboxes sharing a machine mostly run unrelated work for different customers, so they rarely spike at the same moment. If every Sandbox reserved capacity for its peak, the machine would need room for the sum of all the peaks. With bursting, it only needs room for the most they use at the same time. title: WordInferBench: Can Agents Infer How to Edit from Word Document Context?
summary: Document editing is among the most common knowledge-work tasks, yet existing benchmarks for evaluating autonomous agents on Word document editing provide fully specified attribute-modification instructions. They do not evaluate agents' ability to infer the appropriate attributes from document context, a capability essential in real-world editing where users expect consistency without spelling out every attribute. We introduce WordInferBench, a benchmark comprising 280 base document-editing instances, each paired with three instruction conditions: descriptive (the instruction explicitly lists every attribute change), referential (the instruction points to another object as an exemplar), and inferential (the agent must examine document context to infer what attributes to apply). To evaluate contextual attribute inference, each base instance is constructed so that the target formatting is recoverable from an in-document exemplar. The instances are derived from real Word documents collected from Common Crawl and cover 13 object types and 81 attributes. We evaluate six recent coding-agent systems and find that the best-performing evaluated system, Claude Code with Opus 4.6, achieves a 62.9% task-level pass rate on descriptive variants but only 40.7% on inferential variants, indicating that current systems complete tasks less reliably when the required formatting changes must be determined from document context.

title: DecArena: Evaluating Large-Scale Decentralized Multi-Agent Collaboration
summary: Emerging personal AI agents raise fundamental scalability and privacy concerns for centralized multi-agent systems (MASs), which rely on a global orchestrator with broad access to agents, resources, and communication. In decentralized environments, global visibility is unavailable. Agents need to proactively discover non-local resources (e.g. tools, skills), and collaborate with other agents to solve tasks. We study decentralized multi-agent collaboration under graph-constrained communication, a natural reflection of human structures. Each agent observes only its local state and can interact only with neighboring agents. We introduce a benchmark with synthetic scalable distributed tool calling with 100K+ tools. Our experiments reveal that recent LLM agents struggle to discover non-local relevant resources and collaborate in decentralized setting. Moreover, standard reinforcement learning fails to reliably overcome this limitation, suggesting that decentralized MAS needs more explicit harness mechanisms for effective collaboration, even using SOTA LLMs. We then present a strong baseline \textbf{GraphHarness}, combining topology-aware warmup with self-improving LLM-based routing. Results show that GraphHarness substantially improves task success (+48.5) and produces higher quality collaboration (+30.6), while using fewer costs (+34.0) than baselines.

title: CastWorld: Benchmarking Context-Aware Agentic Time Series Forecasting Beyond Predictive Accuracy
summary: Agentic time series forecasting extends conventional approaches beyond one-shot numerical prediction toward autonomous, context-aware interaction. However, existing benchmarks offer limited integrated support for diverse contextual information, forecasting-specific adaptive interactions, and systematic evaluation of forecasting agents. In this paper, we introduce CastWorld, an agentic benchmark for context-aware time series forecasting. First, its context-rich dataset suite spans 8 domains and 25 real-world datasets, covering external variables, events, and historical cases under a unified context specification. Second, a lightweight, modular forecasting-native harness provides 49 core tools and a state-adaptive loop that tracks forecast versions and enables iterative evidence gathering and forecast revision. Intermediate forecasts can expose information gaps, while newly acquired evidence guides subsequent revisions and final version selection. Third, model-level evaluation assesses forecast quality, process execution, behavioral trustworthiness, and resource efficiency through decision trajectories and forecast-version histories. Also, systems-level evaluation compares predictive accuracy across forecasting systems. Experiments reveal distinct decision behaviors among agents with comparable accuracy. Additional interactions do not necessarily improve forecasts, and agents may fail to select their best previously generated predictions. Allowing evidence acquisition during forecast refinement improves task-aware forecast scores across all three evaluated models. CastWorld provides a reusable foundation for evaluating agentic time series forecasting under controlled conditions.

title: What Makes a VLA Reactive? A Study of Execution Strategies for Dynamic Manipulation
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models predict chunks of future actions, and when objects move, those chunks go stale before they are executed. We study what makes a pretrained VLA reactive, using \pihalf{} on two dynamic simulation benchmarks and three real-robot tasks. We vary the prediction and execution horizons, compare synchronous and asynchronous inference, test methods that deliver actions sooner or keep successive chunks continuous, and adapt the policy with motion cues and latent-space reinforcement learning. The best prediction horizon is about one second, and the best execution horizon depends on the checkpoint. Short horizons help more with asynchronous execution, and methods that keep the trajectory continuous outperform those that only reduce latency. Adapting the policy repairs targeted failures, but on the conveyor task changing the execution horizon gained as much. Reactivity depends on the execution pipeline as much as on the policy, so both should be evaluated together.

title: Read Once, Answer Many: Parallel Prompting for Shared-Context LLM Inference
summary: LLM workloads sometimes ask many independent questions about the same long document, as in document QA, data labeling and LLM-based evaluation. Prefix caching removes the redundant prefill shared by these queries, but each decode step still reads the document's key-value (KV) cache once per question, so decoding is bound by memory bandwidth and scales with the number of questions. We present Parallel Prompting, which decodes P questions as P independent streams of a single request all at once, fixing this issue. In our method, every step reads the shared document once for all P streams, and a stream-id attention mask, evaluated inside the attention kernel, keeps each answer conditioned only on the document and its own question. We implement Parallel Prompting in SGLang by adding about 80 lines to three existing files and a small engine package; the mask needs no dense tensor, and every decode step has a fixed shape that is captured as a CUDA graph. With CodeLlama-7B, 8k-16k-token documents and 64-256 questions per document, Parallel Prompting is 3.7x faster than stock SGLang with its FlashInfer backend on an A100 and 5.9-6.0x faster on an RTX A6000, on two SGLang releases, including the most recent release. Timed on identical inputs, it is faster than stock SGLang in all 144 runs (2 GPUs x 2 releases x 6 workloads x 6 input sets). Code: https://github.com/jlab-nlp/parallel-prompting

summary: vLLM supports Thinking Machines' Inkling 2 Small from day 0: attention residuals, a new decode kernel for relative-bias attention, all-reduce fused with the ops around it, and DSpark speculative decoding.
story_key: model:vllm|variant:small|title:inkling 2 small on vllm day 0 support
content_excerpt: vLLM supports Thinking Machines' Inkling 2 Small on day 0. It is a multimodal (text and vision) MoE model with 594B total and 17B active parameters and up to 1M tokens of context. The model also comes with a native DSpark speculator. vLLM supports it with optimized performance (up to 630 TPS/user at TP4 and acceptance length 3.5) and also supports LoRA. Figure 1. Inkling 2 Small architecture. Gold marks what is new or changed since Inkling. Inkling backbone + recent advances. Inkling 2 Small keeps Inkling's backbone: the 5:1 mix of sliding-window and full attention, GQA with a learned relative bias instead of RoPE, the four short convolutions per layer and a sigmoid-routed MoE. On top of it, it adds recent advances. Block attention residuals replace the residual stream, so before each sublayer a learned query mixes the outputs of earlier 6-layer blocks. Gated attention puts a sigmoid gate on each head's output, together with a per-token attention sink . It replaces the hMLP image encoder with a 23-layer ViT. Mixed-precision MoE with Four-Over-Six NVFP4. Out of Inkling 2 Small's 48 layers, the experts of the first 40 use NVFP4 and those of the last 8 use MXFP8. The NVFP4 activations use a per-token global scale plus dual-candidate block scales ( Four Over Six ): for each 16-element block, the quantizer tries scaling the block's maximum to 6 and to 4, and keeps whichever gives the lower reconstruction error (MAE). DSpark speculator with an RNN head. The checkpoint also ships a DSpark draft in place of Inkling's 8 chained MTP heads. The speculator has 5 layers and drafts 7 tokens per step. The head is the RNN variant that DeepSeek's DSpark paper described. Kernel fusion and PDL. vLLM aggressively fuses the collective communication and memory-bound ops between sublayers into a single kernel. With attention residuals, each boundary needs an all-reduce, a short convolution, a residual update, the attention-residual mix and an RMSNorm: five memory-bound steps on the same hidden states. The fused kernel, allreduce_conv_mix (gold in Figure 2), runs the all-reduce over NVLink multicast and keeps everything after it in registers. The GEMM, attention, routing and activation kernels launch with programmatic dependent launch (PDL), so each one's prologue overlaps the tail of the previous kernel, which matters at small batch sizes, where a decode step is a long chain of short kernels. Claude Mythos 5.2 is our most capable model for cybersecurity and life sciences research, available through our verification programs. If you build on the Claude Platform or work in Claude Code, you may be wondering which model to use for your common tasks. This article will help answer that question and how to think about the trade-offs. The quick answer is that you should start most work on Opus 5.5 at its default effort level, medium . There's a reason it's the default model in Claude Code. It costs half as much per input and output token as Fable 5.2, and it's the model we recommend starting with for most coding and knowledge work. Before you move models, try adjusting your effort level. It's a finer dial for both cost and capability. Past high , one more effort level can cost as much as a bigger model, so compare both on your own work. If you're past high , test the next model up at a lower effort instead. Conversely, one level down can get you the result you need at a lower rate. Higher effort helps when the model needs to think longer, call more tools, or check its own work more. Just keep in mind that it also adds latency. Additionally, moving to a higher effort level won't give a model knowledge or skill it doesn't have. For that, you still need to move up a model. Prices are Claude API list prices. For benchmark results, see the Fable 5.2 page . When you choose between models, you're making a trade-off. When you pick a larger model, for example, you are choosing capability over latency. These are the main trade-offs to think through. Generally, bigger models cost more per token and are more capable, but the cost vs capability trade-off isn't universally true at the task level. A higher price per token doesn't always mean a higher cost per task, or a better result. In that time, it generated 1,540 sales artifacts, which reps used to build by hand, one account at a time. Inconsistent versions of the same document were showing up across the org. Account executives built proposal decks by pulling usage data into a chat assistant and assembling the deck themselves. The same work got repeated on every deal, and it looked different every time. We needed a way to standardize our hard-won lessons on what works without slowing anyone down. content_excerpt: Developers, enterprises, scientists, and consumers can now try our latest frontier model. Today, we’re making Gemini 4 Carbon available to developers, enterprises, scientists, and consumers. Carbon is our strongest model with frontier performance in cybersecurity capabilities and long-horizon agentic workflows across complex knowledge work, software engineering, and scientific reasoning. Two weeks ago , we released Carbon to a set of cybersecurity defenders via our Fairwind Program . Following our recent launch of Gemini 4 Argon , Carbon pushes the frontier even further. Argon remains the ideal choice for the majority of software engineering and knowledge work, while Carbon is built for tasks that test the limits of a model’s intelligence like complex, multi-step coding and debugging and open-ended scientific research and discovery — using more tokens than Argon to explore thoroughly, reason deeply, and run extended verification loops. Across independent benchmarks designed to test model performance in real workflows, Carbon pairs frontier accuracy with practical production economics. It ranks #1 on CursorBench 4.0 , Perplexity’s WANDR , and Zapier’s AutomationBench at more than 2X lower cost per task compared to the next best external model. title: Introducing AlphaProof Code: a breakthrough in verifying complex software at depth
summary: AlphaProof Code agents wrote three  million lines of proofs in Lean to verify Signal’s core encryption.
story_key: story|title:introducing alphaproof code a breakthrough in verifying complex software at dept
content_excerpt: How Google DeepMind researchers built a new agentic framework that formally verified the code of Signal’s cryptographic protocol — long considered to be a grand security challenge Today, we’re sharing a milestone in software security long considered to be a grand challenge: Google DeepMind researchers guided AI agents to mathematically prove key security properties of the actual code underlying the Signal protocol, the technology that protects billions of private conversations in apps like Signal and Google Messages. This breakthrough discovery was made using AlphaProof Code , a novel agentic framework for formal verification at unprecedented depth that combines human expertise with AI agents. Formal verification—mathematically proving code runs correctly without flaws—is the highest standard of security assurance; however, it is difficult and often labor-intensive. Our work marks the first time AI has been used to formally verify a widely deployed cryptographic protocol at this depth. It's also the first time the implementation of a widely deployed protocol like this has been formally verified by any method, with or without AI. AlphaProof Code is a multi-LLM agentic framework that splits the work of formal verification the way a research team would: human experts work with AI to decide what to prove, and a group of AI agents does it. First, our researchers collaborated with a mix of models to translate Signal’s security goals into formal mathematical specifications, with human experts reviewing every one. From there, agents powered by Gemini Carbon did the proofs, generating over six million lines of Lean, a computer language that mathematically proves the accuracy of code. Next, the agents audited the proof and highlighted areas that needed a second look by a human – just one percent of the codebase, a massive time savings. Because Lean automatically checks the rest, our experts could focus their review where human judgment matters most. Cryptographic protocols underpin nearly all digital communication, from online banking to web browsing, and a single flaw can expose millions of people at once. That's why experts have spent decades formally analyzing them. But most protocol verification stops at the design level.
